flashcards.q: Which labs define the 2026 frontier, and how do their model families structure output?
flashcards.a: Closed-first: OpenAI (GPT-5.x tiers), Anthropic (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku), Google DeepMind (Gemini Pro/Flash), xAI (Grok). Open-weight: DeepSeek (MIT V-flagship + R-reasoners), Alibaba Qwen, Mistral (dense/MoE/reasoning split), Meta in transition. Every family ships a tier ladder — flagship/workhorse/fast — spanning roughly $1.25-$50/M output tokens with reasoning dials and ~1M contexts.

flashcards.q: What are the five lenses for auditing a model card?
flashcards.a: (1) Evals: cited vs omitted, vendor vs independent, compute tier, checkpoint precision; (2) Data: source taxonomy, cutoff, contamination methodology or silence; (3) License: OSI status, scale thresholds, jurisdictional carve-outs, incorporated policies, output rights; (4) Safety: red-team scope plus who owns residual risk (usually the deployer); (5) Operations: version pinning, static-model notices, output ceilings, compute/emissions disclosure.

flashcards.q: Why is 'open weights' not open source? Cite the concrete failures.
flashcards.a: Open weights answer logistics; open source answers rights. Meta's Llama Community License fails OSI's definition per OSI/FSF analyses: purpose restrictions via an Acceptable Use Policy, discrimination by user class (700M-MAU provision), field-of-endeavor limits, and EU carve-outs in some versions. MIT and Apache 2.0 are the genuine articles.

(1) Non-OSI 'community' licenses masquerading as open; (2) scale thresholds changing terms by who you are (Llama's 700M MAU); (3) jurisdictional carve-outs (EU restrictions); (4) Acceptable Use Policies incorporated by reference and updatable; (5) output-rights variance (Llama 4 explicitly permits synthetic-data/distillation use; others don't); (6) attribution notice-file mechanics.

flashcards.q: Quantify benchmark contamination and why published scores need provenance checks.
flashcards.a: ~29.1% of MMLU items show contamination signals (JHU NAACL 2024), C-Eval ~45.8%, multilingual benchmarks up to ~91.8%. Meta self-reported 16% MMLU overlap in Llama 2 (>80% token match on some items); GPT-4's report admitted 9/34 exams >20% overlap. Impact is real: clean-mirror GSM8K dropped ~13 points; inference-time decontamination removes ~22.9% of MMLU inflation.

flashcards.q: Why do n-gram decontamination filters fail, and what replaces them?
flashcards.a: GPT-3 filtered 13-gram matches, GPT-4 raised to 40-grams — but exact-match filters miss paraphrases, translations, and reformatted tables, which is exactly how multilingual contamination reaches ~92%. Replacements: dynamic benchmarks refreshing from post-cutoff sources (LiveBench monthly), private held-out sets (MMLU-CF: GPT-4o scored 73.4% versus higher public numbers), and inference-time decontamination.

flashcards.q: What does the bf16-vs-quantized evaluation gap look like concretely?
flashcards.a: Llama 4's card states all reported evaluations ran on bf16 models while quantized checkpoints are provided for deployment — meaning the published numbers don't describe the artifact most adopters will serve. Auditors require precision-matched evals or run their own before committing to a serving configuration.

flashcards.q: How do modern model cards handle safety responsibility?
flashcards.a: They transfer residual risk to the deployer: Llama 4's card makes developers responsible for application-specific safety testing and tuning, designates uses beyond 12 supported languages (of ~200 pretrained) or more than 5 input images as out-of-scope unless mitigated, recommends system-level guards (Llama Guard-class), while vendor red-teaming covered three categories (CBRNE, child safety, cyber enablement). Read both halves: what was tested AND what became contractually yours.

flashcards.q: What did the mid-2026 export-control incidents teach about availability?
flashcards.a: That regulatory state is a first-class availability dimension: one flagship was suspended ~22 days post-launch under US export-control directive and another gated ~12 days pending government safety review — with customers mid-dependency. Lessons: tested multi-vendor fallbacks, abstraction layers, regulatory monitoring wired into ops, contracts allocating suspension risk.

flashcards.q: Contrast DeepSeek's and Meta's openness strategies.
flashcards.a: DeepSeek: consistent MIT licensing of frontier-class MoE flagships plus R-series reasoners with published recipes — openness as strategy that reset global pricing and enabled residency-constrained deployments. Meta: openness as instrument — Llama seeded an ecosystem under a non-OSI Community License, then frontier work pivoted closed (Muse Spark API-only) before partial Apache 2.0 reopenings. Lesson: openness is a per-model license property, never a lab identity.

flashcards.q: Why can costs vary ~40x across comparable-capability tiers?
flashcards.a: Positioning margin on flagships vs volume pricing on fast tiers; inference structure (MoE active params, reasoning-token burn at higher effort); bundling (managed safety, SLAs, compliance certifications); strategic anchoring against MIT-licensed competition ($1.25/M floor) while capability-at-any-price buyers sustain premium tiers ($50/M). Decide price-per-task at your quality bar using your private eval, not list-price comparisons.

flashcards.q: Which model-card sections do engineers skip that bite hardest?
flashcards.a: (1) License annexes — incorporated use policies, jurisdictional clauses; (2) out-of-scope limitations (unsupported languages/image counts shift all risk to you); (3) precision/evaluation-conditions footnotes (bf16 vs quantized); (4) static-model/version-semantics notices; (5) data-source disclosures mapping to GDPR/CCPA duties. Ownership: joint engineering+legal on ONE worksheet artifact with a blocking gate.

flashcards.q: Describe disclosure asymmetry across labs and why third-party trackers matter.
flashcards.a: Third-party trackers score labs on disclosed specs/benchmarks ranging from full disclosure (~8/8 for one major lab) down to effectively zero (qualitative launch copy only), with conflicting numbers even for shipped flagships (same model scoring 88.0% vs 83.4% on Terminal-Bench across harnesses). Vendor blogs are marketing-grade until independently confirmed — trackers normalize provenance.

(1) Define task metric that matters (task completion, not leaderboard proxy); (2) filter by hard constraints — license/residency/deployment mode eliminates fastest; (3) evaluate top-3 on YOUR private eval set; (4) price the tier portfolio with routing economics; (5) negotiate exit paths and test fallback quarterly. Indefensible: brand loyalty, benchmark tweets, single-model bets.

flashcards.q: What belongs in an organizational model-adoption policy?
flashcards.a: Seven clauses: mandatory teardown-worksheet gate before data-touching pilots; license whitelist logic (MIT/Apache pass, community licenses route to legal); private-eval minimum bars per task class with recorded results; precision-matched eval requirements; version-pinning and rotation-diff obligations; data-provenance-to-privacy mapping at adoption; exit-path requirements with tested second-vendor fallback. Tier rigor by exposure so prototype speed survives.
